market_definition.category: Payroll and workforce-compliance delivery for agricultural employers in North America. The economically meaningful unit is not 'agricultural payroll software' but 'how a farm employer gets payroll and seasonal labour compliance done at all' — a question answered three different ways: a payroll module bundled inside a farm-management ERP [S2], a professional employer organisation that performs payroll as a service [S3], or a purpose-built agricultural payroll product [S1].
market_definition.boundary_notes: Drawing the boundary at 'software vendors built for agricultural payroll' produces a two-company market [S1]; drawing it at 'agricultural employers who must run payroll' produces a market in which those two companies together hold an estimated 6-9% of employers and the majority is served by ERP bundles or PEOs [S1]. The second boundary is the correct one, because S1 reports the common buyer shortlist is the incumbent farm-management ERP against a PEO, and that a specialist payroll vendor appears in only a minority of evaluations [S1] — meaning most of the demand is decided in a room where no specialist product is present. Note also that the deck's stated expansion segment (specialty crop growers) is not separately sized, characterised, or distinguished from general agricultural employers anywhere in this bibliography; I could not verify whether it behaves as a distinct market. Nothing in the material describes the whole-category size in dollars, employer counts, or seats, so every statement here about proportions is a share statement, not a size statement.
how_analysts_segment_it: By delivery mode: bundled ERP payroll module vs. PEO-as-a-service vs. standalone specialist software [S1][S2][S3]
By pay structure supported: hourly only vs. hourly plus piece-rate — S2 reports leading ERP payroll modules handle hourly and, in recent releases, piece-rate [S2]
By regulatory coverage, specifically H-2A wage-rate requirements, which S2 identifies as the most frequently cited gap in ERP modules [S2]
By workforce seasonality — S3 segments on size of seasonal intake, noting PEO adoption is highest among employers running large seasonal intakes [S3]
Inferred, not read from a source: no source in this bibliography segments by crop type, acreage, geography within North America, or by specialty-crop vs. row-crop

sizing.consensus_view: There is no consensus view because there are no estimates. Not one source in this bibliography states a TAM, SAM, SOM, revenue figure, employer count, worker count, or spend-per-employer for agricultural payroll in North America. The only quantity anywhere in the material is a share: AgriPay and HarvestHR together hold an estimated 6-9% of agricultural employers [S1]. That figure is a denominator-free share of employers, not of dollars, and S1 does not state the denominator's size or how the estimate was derived. Any dollar figure I produced here would be fabricated, so I produce none.
sizing.cagr_range: No source states a growth rate for this category. The only directional signal in the material is a capability trend, not a market-growth trend: ERP payroll modules have added piece-rate support in recent releases [S2].
sizing.why_estimates_diverge: Estimates cannot diverge because none were provided. The absence is itself informative in two ways. First, it means the deck's decision to state the market as a category name with no TAM/SAM/SOM and no methodology [C9] cannot be checked against anything — I have no independent number to hold it to. Second, if this category were being actively sized by analyst houses or vendors, at least one such figure would normally surface in a landscape search; the bibliography here was assembled from four queries all on the theme of agricultural payroll software vendors and returned zero sizing material, which is weak evidence that the category is small enough or obscure enough not to be routinely sized. I flag that as an inference from absence, which is the weakest kind of evidence, and I do not build on it.

tailwinds: Real, structural pay-mechanics complexity: agricultural payroll combines piece-rate and hourly work and H-2A wage-rate rules, and S2 confirms from the supply side that H-2A wage-rate coverage 'varies' among ERP modules and is 'the most frequently cited gap' [S2] — an independently observed unmet need, not a founder assertion

Seasonality creates concentrated operational pain: S3 reports the employers with large seasonal intakes are the same profile that experiences the most acute payroll complexity [S3], so the pain is genuine and is concentrated in an identifiable segment
Piece-rate support is recent in ERP modules rather than long-established [S2], which implies a period during which specialist products were the only way to express it
headwinds: The specialist product is usually not in the room: S1 reports a specialist payroll vendor appears in a minority of evaluations, and the common shortlist is the incumbent farm-management ERP against a PEO [S1]. This is a demand-access problem, not a product problem, and it is the single most important finding in this bibliography

Default adoption defeats selection: S2 states the ERP payroll module is 'adopted by default rather than selected' [S2]. A buyer who never runs an evaluation cannot be won by being better in an evaluation

The highest-pain segment is already served by a substitute: PEO adoption is highest among large-seasonal-intake employers [S3], i.e. the customers with the most acute complexity are disproportionately the ones who have already outsourced the whole problem rather than bought software for it

Two specialist vendors together reach only an estimated 6-9% of agricultural employers [S1] after however many years they have existed — the material does not say how long, but the low ceiling is evidence that specialist software has historically struggled to convert this buyer

PEOs absorb payroll, workers compensation and seasonal compliance together [S3]. A software product that solves only payroll is competing against a bundle that also removes the employer's workers-comp and compliance burden
demand_signals.buyer_budget_reality: Inferred from the structure S1-S3 describe, not stated in any source: for the majority of agricultural employers the payroll budget is already committed — either sunk into a farm-management ERP the office already operates, where the payroll module arrives bundled and is adopted by default [S2], or spent as a PEO service fee that also covers workers compensation and seasonal compliance [S3]. In both cases a specialist payroll product is incremental spend displacing something already paid for, not a new line item. No source states what any of these three options costs, what a farm employer spends on payroll annually, or whether the specialist commands a premium or a discount, so I cannot say whether the displacement is economically easy or hard.

incumbents.name: Farm-management ERP platforms (unnamed in this bibliography)
incumbents.position: The default channel. S2 reports that the leading farm-management ERP platforms ship payroll modules handling hourly and, in recent releases, piece-rate pay, and that because the module is bundled with a system the farm office already operates, it is adopted by default rather than selected [S2]. S1 corroborates from the demand side: a farm-management ERP is one of the two options on the common buyer shortlist [S1]. Their acknowledged weakness is H-2A wage-rate coverage, which varies by platform and is the most frequently cited gap [S2]. This is the category of competitor that would not appear on a startup's competitive matrix and is nonetheless the one that decides most of the market.

incumbents.name: Professional employer organisations serving agriculture (unnamed in this bibliography)
incumbents.position: A service substitute rather than a software competitor, and therefore easy to omit from a software competitive matrix. S3 reports PEOs absorb payroll, workers compensation and seasonal compliance as a service, with adoption highest among employers running large seasonal intakes — the profile with the most acute payroll complexity [S3]. S1 places a PEO on the common shortlist alongside the incumbent ERP [S1]. The strategic significance is that PEOs are strongest precisely where a piece-rate/H-2A/seasonal-intake product claims its sharpest differentiation.

challengers.name: AgriPay
challengers.position: One of two software vendors S1 identifies as built specifically for agricultural payroll; together with HarvestHR it holds an estimated 6-9% of agricultural employers [S1]. No source states its funding, headcount, revenue, product capabilities, H-2A coverage, or pricing, and no source splits the 6-9% between the two vendors.

challengers.name: HarvestHR
challengers.position: The second of the two purpose-built agricultural payroll vendors identified by S1, sharing the estimated combined 6-9% employer share [S1]. As with AgriPay, no funding, scale, capability or pricing detail appears anywhere in this bibliography.

adjacent_threats: Farm-management ERP vendors extending payroll depth — piece-rate has already arrived in recent releases [S2], and the remaining differentiator named by the source is H-2A wage-rate coverage, a defined regulatory requirement rather than an open-ended capability, which makes it a closable gap rather than a permanent one
PEOs moving further up the complexity curve, since they already own the large-seasonal-intake employer and already bundle workers compensation and seasonal compliance with payroll [S3]

Inferred, unsupported by any source here: general-purpose payroll and HR platforms, farm labour contractors, and agricultural accounting software are all plausible adjacent entrants, but this bibliography contains no evidence about any of them and I will not assert their presence
differentiation_axes: H-2A wage-rate compliance coverage — the most frequently cited gap in incumbent ERP modules [S2], and therefore the axis on which a specialist has the clearest claim
Piece-rate pay expression, now partially neutralised as a differentiator by recent ERP releases [S2]
Handling of large seasonal intakes — the operational profile S3 associates with the most acute complexity [S3]
Delivery model: software the farm office runs vs. a service that removes the work entirely [S3]

Distribution and default position — S2's observation that the ERP module is adopted by default rather than selected [S2] makes incumbency itself a competitive axis, and on the evidence the decisive one [S1]
Bundle breadth: payroll alone vs. payroll plus workers compensation plus seasonal compliance [S3]

saturation.consolidation_activity: None seen. No source in this bibliography reports any acquisition, merger, investment, shutdown or exit in agricultural payroll software. This is an absence of reported activity in a four-source bibliography, not verified evidence that none occurred.
saturation.why: The evidence, stated precisely. On specialist-vendor count: S1 names exactly two software vendors built for this market — AgriPay and HarvestHR [S1] — and I found no third. On funding: no source states a funding round, amount, date or investor for any player in this category, so I cannot report that I found any funded competitors; I set the count to null rather than report '2' and imply funding evidence I do not have. On entrant flow: unknown — the bibliography contains no dated entrant or round data, so I cannot distinguish 'no new entrants in two years' from 'entrants exist but were not captured by these four queries'. On pricing: unknown — no source states a price, a discount, or a direction. On the niche read: the case for room is that H-2A wage-rate coverage varies across incumbent ERP modules and is the most frequently cited gap [S2], which is an independently observed, specific, unserved requirement — that is a real wedge, and only two specialists are pursuing it [S1]. The case against is stronger than the vendor count suggests and does not depend on saturation at all: the two specialists together reach only an estimated 6-9% of agricultural employers [S1], a specialist appears in only a minority of evaluations [S1], and the incumbent module is adopted by default rather than selected [S2]. So this category is uncrowded and simultaneously hard to sell into. The binding constraint is access to the buyer, not competition for the buyer — which is why a low competitor count should not be read here as an open market.

likely_absorbers.name: Farm-management ERP platforms
likely_absorbers.why_them: They already own the system the farm office operates daily, they already ship a payroll module inside it, and S2 states explicitly that this bundling causes the module to be 'adopted by default rather than selected' [S2]. That is the absorption mechanism operating already — the customer relationship, the distribution and the default are all in place, and only capability depth is missing. The gap is narrow and named: H-2A wage-rate coverage 'varies' and is the most frequently cited gap [S2]. H-2A wage rates are a defined regulatory requirement, which makes this a specification to implement rather than an open-ended capability race.
signals_already_visible: Shipped feature: ERP payroll modules now handle piece-rate pay in recent releases [S2] — a capability the deck treats as its own differentiator has already appeared in the incumbent bundle
Structural signal: the module is adopted by default rather than selected [S2], meaning absorption does not require the incumbent to win an evaluation
Demand-side confirmation: the incumbent farm-management ERP is one of the two options on the common buyer shortlist, while a specialist appears in only a minority of evaluations [S1]

Not found: no job postings, roadmap statements, H-2A-specific release notes, or acquisition activity appear anywhere in this bibliography — the absorption read rests on the shipped piece-rate feature and the default-adoption dynamic only

likely_absorbers.name: Professional employer organisations serving agriculture
likely_absorbers.why_them: Absorption here is by service substitution rather than software bundling. S3 reports PEOs already absorb payroll, workers compensation and seasonal compliance as a single service, and that adoption is highest among employers running large seasonal intakes — the same profile that experiences the most acute payroll complexity [S3]. The customer with the strongest reason to buy a specialist product is therefore disproportionately likely to have already handed the entire function to a PEO. A PEO does not need to build piece-rate or H-2A logic to take the account; it takes the account by removing the employer's need to operate any of it.
signals_already_visible: Already shipped, in the sense that matters: PEOs serve this exact function today, including seasonal compliance, not as a roadmap item [S3]
Concentration of PEO adoption in the highest-complexity, largest-seasonal-intake segment [S3] — the segment a specialist product would target first
Not found: no source reports PEO pricing, PEO market share among agricultural employers, or whether PEO adoption in agriculture is growing or flat

precedents.category: Payroll as a module inside vertical ERP suites generally
precedents.absorbed_by: The vertical ERP that already owns the back office
precedents.how_long_it_took: Not stated in any source in this bibliography
precedents.why_it_is_comparable: Flagged explicitly: no source in this bibliography documents this precedent, so the source_ids array is empty and this entry is reasoning, not evidence. The mechanism match is nonetheless exact and observable in the material itself — S2 describes the mechanism in progress (bundled module, default adoption, capability gap narrowing as piece-rate ships) rather than by analogy [S2]. I include it only because the mechanism is visible here directly; I decline to cite the usual absorption precedents (antivirus, file sync, VPN, password management) because none of them appear in this bibliography and none involve a regulated pay-calculation requirement, so the mechanism match would be decorative.

what_would_prevent_it: A genuine regulatory moat around H-2A wage-rate compliance — but only if certification, audit, attestation or liability transfer is involved. S2 describes H-2A coverage as varying and frequently gapped [S2], which suggests it is currently a depth-of-implementation problem rather than a licensed or accredited one. No source in this bibliography states that any certification, audit regime or attestation exists for agricultural payroll compliance software, so I cannot confirm this moat exists. This is the single most important unverified question in the whole analysis, because it is the difference between a defensible category and a feature ERPs will finish building

Regulatory change velocity: if H-2A wage rates and related rules change often enough that maintaining correctness is a continuous operational burden rather than a one-time build, an ERP vendor for whom payroll is one module among many may not sustain it. No source states how often these rules change, so this is a hypothesis

Workflow depth at the seasonal intake peak — onboarding hundreds of workers in a compressed window is an operational load an ERP module may not have been built for. S3 confirms large seasonal intakes correlate with the most acute complexity [S3], but no source assesses whether incumbent products handle intake volume, so the depth of this moat is unverified

A buyer who will not consolidate — no evidence for this exists in the material; on the contrary, S2's 'adopted by default' finding [S2] and S1's shortlist finding [S1] both indicate a buyer who consolidates readily and does not run competitive evaluations
absorption_risk.notes: The verdict is 'contested' rather than 'feature' for one reason: the residual gap that S2 names — H-2A wage-rate coverage [S2] — is real, independently observed, and currently unclosed across the incumbent field. It is contested rather than 'product' because everything else the deck describes as differentiation has either already shipped in the bundle (piece-rate [S2]) or is already served by a substitute at exactly the customer profile where it matters most (large seasonal intake, PEOs [S3]). The honest framing: this is a category whose defensibility rests almost entirely on one regulatory capability, and whose defensibility therefore lasts exactly as long as that capability is hard. I could not verify whether it is hard, which is why confidence is medium rather than high. A separate observation on evaluation-based evidence: S4 states plainly that no independent source publishes head-to-head win rates for agricultural payroll vendors, and that vendor-reported win rates in adjacent categories have been found to describe only the deals a vendor was invited into, excluding decisions where no specialist was shortlisted at all [S4]. Read alongside S1's finding that a specialist appears in only a minority of evaluations [S1], any win-rate figure in this category measures performance inside the minority of deals a specialist reached, and is structurally silent about the majority. That is a market-structure fact about how evidence works here; whether a particular deck over-reads such a figure is for the next stage to judge.

open_source_landscape.evidence_for_the_gap: No source in this bibliography names an open-source agricultural payroll project, an open-source payroll engine, an open-source H-2A wage-rate or piece-rate calculation library, or any community effort in this space. The four sources describe only commercial delivery modes: purpose-built vendors [S1], bundled ERP modules [S2] and PEO services [S3]. The 'far behind' value is therefore an artefact of the schema requiring a value, not a measured assessment — it should be read as 'no open-source alternative was found in the provided material', and I am flagging that rather than dressing an absence as a finding. Structurally, I would note that the competitive threat in this category comes from bundling and service substitution rather than from free software, and that payroll is a domain where liability for getting a regulated calculation wrong sits with the employer, which historically discourages unsupported free tooling — but that is reasoning, not evidence from any source here.

what_commercial_still_provides.capability: H-2A wage-rate compliance implementation and its ongoing maintenance
what_commercial_still_provides.why: S2 identifies H-2A wage-rate coverage as the most frequently cited gap in incumbent ERP payroll modules [S2] — so it is currently a genuine differentiator. It is marked not durable because it is a defined regulatory specification rather than an accumulating asset: an ERP vendor that decides to close it can close it, and no source states that any certification, audit or attestation barrier stands in the way. If such a barrier exists, this assessment flips, which is why I list it as the top research gap.

what_commercial_still_provides.capability: Combined piece-rate and hourly pay processing
what_commercial_still_provides.why: Already replicated in the bundle: S2 reports leading farm-management ERP platforms handle hourly and, in recent releases, piece-rate pay [S2]. A capability the incumbent has already shipped is by definition cheaply replicable by that incumbent.

what_commercial_still_provides.capability: Service absorption of the whole payroll and seasonal-compliance function
what_commercial_still_provides.why: Not a software moat at all, and already provided by a different delivery model — PEOs absorb payroll, workers compensation and seasonal compliance as a service [S3]. A software vendor cannot claim this as residual value because a competing model already offers it more completely.

open_source_landscape.notes: Set to not applicable deliberately rather than inventing an open-source dimension, per instruction. The absorption mechanism that actually threatens this category is suite bundling by an incumbent that already owns the customer relationship and the default [S1][S2], plus service substitution by PEOs [S3] — not open-source commoditisation. Analysts reaching for the Kubernetes/Docker or Snowflake framings should note that neither applies: there is no free alternative here to reach parity with, and the residual gap is regulatory implementation depth held by a vendor that does not own distribution — the reverse of the Snowflake position.

adjacent_markets.why_it_matters: This is the primary channel through which agricultural employers obtain payroll [S1], and its payroll modules are actively deepening — hourly historically, piece-rate in recent releases [S2]. Convergence is one-directional and unfavourable: the ERP is moving into payroll depth from a position of owning the customer, while a payroll specialist moving into farm management would have to displace an operating system of record. A specialist here is pulled into competition with this market whether or not it chooses to be, and S2's 'adopted by default rather than selected' finding [S2] means it competes on unfavourable terms.

adjacent_markets.market: PEO services for agriculture (payroll, workers compensation and seasonal compliance delivered as a service)
adjacent_markets.why_it_matters: A direct substitute that removes the buying decision rather than winning it. It is strongest in the segment with the most acute payroll complexity and the largest seasonal intakes [S3] — the exact segment a piece-rate/H-2A/large-intake product is designed for. Any go-to-market that targets high-complexity farms first will meet a PEO, not a software vendor, and will be arguing about delivery model rather than features.

adjacent_markets.market: Workers compensation and seasonal labour compliance administration
adjacent_markets.why_it_matters: S3 shows these are already bundled with payroll in the PEO offer [S3]. That cuts two ways: it is the natural adjacency for a payroll specialist to expand into in order to match the substitute's bundle breadth, and it is simultaneously proof that a payroll-only product is a narrower offer than what the highest-value segment already buys. No source states the size, margin structure, or licensing requirements of this adjacency.

adjacent_markets.market: H-2A programme administration and agricultural labour supply
adjacent_markets.why_it_matters: H-2A wage-rate requirements are the source of the compliance requirement that defines the specialist wedge [S2] and, per the deck's own framing, the regulatory regime the product claims to encode. Demand for the differentiating capability is therefore downstream of the H-2A programme's scale and rule stability. No source in this bibliography describes the H-2A programme's size, participation trend, or rule-change frequency, so the durability of the wedge cannot be assessed from this material.

economics.typical_pricing: Not stated in any source. No price, price range, pricing model (per-employee-per-month, per-pay-run, percentage-of-payroll), discount trend, or contract length appears anywhere in this bibliography for specialist vendors, ERP payroll modules, or PEO services. This is a material gap: without PEO service-fee comparators there is no way to establish the price ceiling a software product faces from the substitute [S3].
economics.typical_gross_margin: Not stated in any source. Inference only, flagged as such: a software product would be expected to carry materially higher gross margin than a PEO, which performs the function as a service and carries the labour cost of doing so [S3] — but no source states margin for either model, and seasonal compliance support load at intake peaks could compress software margins in ways the material does not let me quantify.
economics.typical_cac_payback: Not stated in any source, and no source provides CAC, sales-cycle length, ACV, or churn for any player. The material does support one directional inference, which I flag as inference: S1 reports that a specialist payroll vendor appears in a minority of evaluations and that the common shortlist is the incumbent ERP against a PEO [S1], while S2 reports the ERP module is adopted by default rather than selected [S2]. A vendor that must first create an evaluation that would not otherwise happen, and only then win it, carries demand-creation cost on top of competitive-selling cost. That structure points toward long payback, but no figure in this bibliography confirms it.

funding_environment.valuation_norms: No source in this bibliography reports a valuation, revenue multiple, round size, or comparable transaction for agricultural payroll software. The deck's $15M at $90M post [C10] therefore has no external comparator in this material, and I decline to manufacture one.
funding_environment.notes: The 'steady' value should be read as not-evidenced rather than as a finding. The schema requires one of hot/steady/cooling/cold and offers no 'unknown', so I chose the least assertive option and am flagging it here explicitly: zero funding rounds, zero acquisitions, zero valuations and zero exits for this category appear anywhere in the four sources provided [S1][S2][S3][S4]. Nothing in this analysis should be built on this field. The genuine finding about capital in this category is negative-space: a landscape search across four vendor-focused queries surfaced no funding or M&A activity at all, which is consistent with either a small, quietly-served niche or with an incomplete bibliography, and I cannot distinguish the two.

factors: H-2A wage-rate requirements are the defining regulatory feature of this category and the most frequently cited gap in incumbent ERP payroll modules [S2]. They are both the specialist's wedge and its dependency

Compliance correctness is a liability question for the employer, which is structurally why PEOs — who take the function on as a service alongside workers compensation and seasonal compliance [S3] — are a credible substitute rather than merely an outsourcing convenience

Piece-rate pay interacts with wage-floor rules in ways that make correctness non-obvious; S2 treats piece-rate as a distinct capability that ERP modules only recently added [S2], indicating it is not trivial to implement
Seasonality concentrates both operational and compliance risk into short intake windows [S3], meaning failures are correlated and time-critical rather than spread evenly

Unverified and important: no source in this bibliography states that any certification, accreditation, audit regime, or attestation standard exists for H-2A or agricultural payroll compliance software. A claim that such compliance is 'built in' [C11] therefore has, in this material, no external mechanism against which it could be validated by a buyer or by an analyst — I could find no such mechanism, which is different from establishing that none exists

Multi-jurisdiction exposure across North America is asserted by the deck; no source in this bibliography describes state, provincial or federal variation in agricultural payroll rules, so I cannot corroborate or size it

sources.title: Who actually sells payroll to agricultural employers
sources.what_it_supported: The identification of AgriPay and HarvestHR as the two purpose-built agricultural payroll vendors; their estimated combined 6-9% share of agricultural employers; the finding that the majority of farm employers obtain payroll bundled with a farm-management ERP or through a PEO; and the buying-process finding that a specialist appears in a minority of evaluations while the common shortlist is the incumbent ERP against a PEO. Rated secondary, not primary: it is a research summary page with no named author, no regulator or company filing behind it, and it attributes its share figure only as an 'estimate' and its shortlist finding only to unnamed 'surveys of buying processes', neither of which can be traced or independently checked from what is provided. It is the single most load-bearing source in this analysis, which makes its unattributed methodology the analysis's central weakness.

sources.title: Farm-management ERP payroll modules
sources.what_it_supported: That leading farm-management ERP platforms ship payroll modules covering hourly and, in recent releases, piece-rate pay; that H-2A wage-rate coverage varies across them and is the most frequently cited gap; and that the module is adopted by default rather than selected because it is bundled with a system the farm office already operates. Rated secondary: a research summary with no named ERP vendors, no release notes, no version dates and no primary vendor documentation cited. The absence of vendor names materially limits the analysis — it means I can describe the incumbent category but cannot verify any individual incumbent's actual H-2A coverage.

sources.title: PEOs in agriculture
sources.what_it_supported: That PEOs serving agriculture absorb payroll, workers compensation and seasonal compliance as a service, and that adoption is highest among employers running large seasonal intakes — the same profile experiencing the most acute payroll complexity. This underpins the substitute-competition and highest-pain-already-served findings. Rated secondary: a research summary with no named PEOs, no share figures, no pricing and no trend data.

sources.title: No published win-rate data exists for this category
sources.what_it_supported: The negative finding that no independent source publishes head-to-head win rates for agricultural payroll vendors, and the methodological finding that vendor-reported win rates in adjacent categories have been found to describe only deals the vendor was invited into, excluding decisions where no specialist was shortlisted. Rated secondary: it reports a methodological pattern from unnamed 'adjacent categories' without naming the studies, vendors or categories involved. A negative finding of this kind is nonetheless useful, because it establishes that the absence of independent win-rate data is a property of the category rather than a gap in my search.

research_gaps: Whole-category sizing: no TAM, SAM, SOM, revenue figure, employer count, worker count, or spend-per-employer appears in any source. Everything quantitative in this bibliography reduces to one estimated share range, 6-9% of agricultural employers held jointly by two vendors [S1], with no stated denominator and no stated methodology. Sizing confidence is low as a direct consequence

Whether any certification, audit, accreditation or attestation regime exists for H-2A wage-rate compliance in payroll software. This is the highest-value unanswered question in the analysis: it determines whether the specialist wedge S2 identifies [S2] is a durable regulatory moat or a feature backlog item for ERP vendors, and therefore whether the absorption verdict should be 'contested' or 'feature'

The identities of the leading farm-management ERP platforms. S2 describes their behaviour but names none [S2], so the most consequential competitor group in this market cannot be examined at the level of individual vendors, roadmaps, release notes, job postings or actual H-2A coverage
The identities and scale of PEOs serving agriculture, their pricing, and whether their agricultural adoption is growing, flat or declining [S3]

Funding, revenue, headcount, customer count and product capability for AgriPay and HarvestHR individually — S1 gives only a combined share [S1]. Without this, I cannot assess whether the two named specialists are well-capitalised competitors or subscale incumbents
All pricing in every delivery mode: specialist software, ERP payroll module, PEO service fee. Without PEO fees in particular there is no observable price ceiling for the substitute

New-entrant flow and dated funding activity, which is why the saturation read reports 'unknown' for entrant trend and pricing direction rather than guessing. I cannot distinguish a category no one is entering from a category these four queries failed to observe entrants in
Any acquisition, exit, or consolidation event in agricultural payroll software

Whether specialty crop growers — the deck's stated expansion target — constitute a distinct segment with different payroll mechanics, regulatory exposure, buying behaviour or vendor landscape. No source in this bibliography addresses specialty crops at all, so the entire expansion thesis sits on unresearched ground
Multi-jurisdiction complexity: no source describes state/provincial/federal variation in agricultural payroll rules across North America, or how often H-2A wage rates change
Independent evidence bearing on competitive win rates in this category — S4 establishes affirmatively that none is published [S4], so this gap is closed as unclosable rather than merely unsearched

Source-quality gap that colours everything above: all four sources are undated-authorship research summaries on a single domain (research.example.org), dated 2026-03, surfaced by variants of one query. Not one primary source — no regulator filing, no public company disclosure, no vendor documentation, no named survey — appears in this bibliography. Under my own source-ranking standard, this analysis rests entirely on the middle tier
